claim: Toxoplasma gondii causes a long-term latent infection of neurons.
source: Toxoplasma gondii is an intracellular parasite that causes a long-term latent infection of neurons.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about Toxoplasma gondii infection, supported by scientific consensus and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Toxoplasma-injected neurons (TINs) are heterogeneously distributed in the brain.
source: Using a custom MATLAB-based mapping program in combination with a mouse model that allows us to permanently mark neurons injected with parasite proteins, we found that Toxoplasma-injected neurons (TINs) are heterogeneously distributed in the brain, primarily localizing to the cortex followed by the striatum.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the MATLAB-based mapping program and mouse model experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: TINs primarily localize to the cortex followed by the striatum.
source: Using a custom MATLAB-based mapping program in combination with a mouse model that allows us to permanently mark neurons injected with parasite proteins, we found that Toxoplasma-injected neurons (TINs) are heterogeneously distributed in the brain, primarily localizing to the cortex followed by the striatum.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B and described in the text.

claim: Cortical TINs are commonly (>50%) excitatory neurons (FoxP2+).
source: In addition, we determined that cortical TINs are commonly (>50%) excitatory neurons (FoxP2+) and that striatal TINs are often (>65%) medium spiny neurons (MSNs) (FoxP2+).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescent assay data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Striatal TINs are often (>65%) medium spiny neurons (MSNs) (FoxP2+).
source: In addition, we determined that cortical TINs are commonly (>50%) excitatory neurons (FoxP2+) and that striatal TINs are often (>65%) medium spiny neurons (MSNs) (FoxP2+).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescent assay data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: TINs have highly aberrant electrophysiology.
source: By performing single neuron patch clamping on striatal TINs and neighboring uninfected MSNs, we discovered that TINs have highly aberrant electrophysiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Approximately 90% of TINs will die by 8 weeks post-infection.
source: As approximately 90% of TINs will die by 8 weeks post-infection, this abnormal physiology suggests that injection with Toxoplasma protein—either directly or indirectly—affects neuronal health and survival.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 comparing TIN counts at 3 and 8 weeks post-infection.

claim: Injection with Toxoplasma protein affects neuronal health and survival.
source: As approximately 90% of TINs will die by 8 weeks post-infection, this abnormal physiology suggests that injection with Toxoplasma protein—either directly or indirectly—affects neuronal health and survival.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of aberrant electrophysiology data and the observed death of TINs over time.

claim: Measles virus causes debilitating disease or death.
source: Most of these viruses cause debilitating disease or death, whereas alphaherpes viruses and the eukaryotic parasite Toxoplasma primarily establish persistent, relatively quiescent neuronal infections in the immunocompetent host (Dubey, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Alphaherpes viruses establish persistent, relatively quiescent neuronal infections in the immunocompetent host.
source: Most of these viruses cause debilitating disease or death, whereas alphaherpes viruses and the eukaryotic parasite Toxoplasma primarily establish persistent, relatively quiescent neuronal infections in the immunocompetent host (Dubey, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Toxoplasma primarily establishes persistent, relatively quiescent neuronal infections in the immunocompetent host.
source: Most of these viruses cause debilitating disease or death, whereas alphaherpes viruses and the eukaryotic parasite Toxoplasma primarily establish persistent, relatively quiescent neuronal infections in the immunocompetent host (Dubey, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established scientific knowledge.

claim: Toxoplasma is a ubiquitous intracellular parasite that can infect a wide range of warm-blooded hosts, including birds, rodents, and humans.
source: Toxoplasma is a ubiquitous intracellular parasite that can infect a wide range of warm-blooded hosts, including birds, rodents, and humans.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Toxoplasma gondii.

claim: In humans and rodents, the CNS is a major organ of persistence for Toxoplasma.
source: In humans and rodents, the CNS is a major organ of persistence and is the organ most affected by symptomatic disease in immunocompromised patients (Remington and Cavanaugh, 1965; Luft and Remington, 1992; Dubey, 2009; Neu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The CNS is the organ most affected by symptomatic Toxoplasma disease in immunocompromised patients.
source: In humans and rodents, the CNS is a major organ of persistence and is the organ most affected by symptomatic disease in immunocompromised patients (Remington and Cavanaugh, 1965; Luft and Remington, 1992; Dubey, 2009; Neu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Toxoplasma predominantly interacts with neurons, not glia, in vivo.
source: Using a Cre-based mouse model in which host cells injected with Toxoplasma protein permanently express a green fluorescent protein (GFP), our group showed that Toxoplasma predominantly interacts with neurons, not glia, in vivo (Koshy et al., 2012; Cabral et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors' group.

claim: Neurons injected with Toxoplasma protein outnumber cysts by over 20-fold.
source: In addition, we determined that neurons injected with Toxoplasma protein outnumber cysts by over 20-fold (Koshy et al., 2012), suggesting that far more neurons interact with Toxoplasma than are persistently infected.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Far more neurons interact with Toxoplasma than are persistently infected.
source: In addition, we determined that neurons injected with Toxoplasma protein outnumber cysts by over 20-fold (Koshy et al., 2012), suggesting that far more neurons interact with Toxoplasma than are persistently infected.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TINs outnumber cysts by over 20-fold.

claim: TINs are most commonly found within the cortex followed by the striatum and are rarely found in the cerebellum.
source: These studies revealed that TINs are most commonly found within the cortex followed by the striatum and are rarely found in the cerebellum.
evidence: This claim is supported by the neuroanatomic mapping data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The lineage of TINs essentially mirrors regional neuron subtype abundance.
source: Within the cortex and the striatum, we used immunofluorescent assays to determine if Toxoplasma preferentially interacts with specific neuron subtypes, finding instead that the lineage of TINs essentially mirrors regional neuron subtype abundance.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescent assay data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: TINs have dramatically altered electrophysiology compared to bystander neurons.
source: These first-of-their-kind studies for any neurotropic microbe showed that TINs—but not bystander neurons—had dramatically altered electrophysiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Bystander neurons do not have dramatically altered electrophysiology.
source: These first-of-their-kind studies for any neurotropic microbe showed that TINs—but not bystander neurons—had dramatically altered electrophysiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by patch clamp data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The number of TINs drops by approximately 90% at 8 weeks post-infection.
source: At 8 weeks post-infection (wpi), the number of TINs drops by approximately 90%, suggesting this abnormal physiology reflects an unhealthy cellular state.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The abnormal physiology of TINs reflects an unhealthy cellular state.
source: At 8 weeks post-infection (wpi), the number of TINs drops by approximately 90%, suggesting this abnormal physiology reflects an unhealthy cellular state.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TINs die over time and have aberrant electrophysiology.

claim: Prior work in AIDS patients and rodents suggested that Toxoplasma does not evenly distribute across the brain.
source: Prior work in AIDS patients and rodents suggested that Toxoplasma does not evenly distribute across the brain (Post et al., 1983; Lang et al., 1989; Luft and Remington, 1992; Arendt et al., 1999; Porter and Sande, 1992; Strittmatter et al., 1992; Berenreiterová et al., 2011; Evans et al., 2014; Neu et al., 2015; Dubey et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: For both II-Cre and III-Cre infected mice, the cortex contained the highest average number of TINs, followed by the striatum.
source: For both II-Cre and III-Cre infected mice, the cortex contained the highest average number of TINs, followed by the striatum (Figure 1A,B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: III-Cre infected mice showed a higher overall number of TINs compared to II-Cre infected mice (average of 247.5 III-Cre versus 216.7 II-Cre).
source: In general, III-Cre infected mice showed a higher overall number of TINs compared to II-Cre infected mice (average of 247.5 III-Cre versus 216.7 II-Cre).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mapping studies.

claim: The increase in absolute numbers of TINs in III-Cre infected mice was most pronounced in the cortex.
source: The increase in absolute numbers in III-Cre infected mice was most pronounced in the cortex (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Most brain regions, including the cerebellum, contained relatively few TINs.
source: Most other brain regions, including the cerebellum, contained relatively few TINs (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The cortex was the only region which was significantly enriched for TINs in both II-Cre and III-Cre infected mice (index score 1.4 ± 0.1 and 2.2 ± 0.2, respectively).
source: Using this normalization, we determined that the cortex was the only region which was significantly enriched for TINs in both II-Cre and III-Cre infected mice (index score 1.4 ± 0.1 and 2.2 ± 0.2, respectively) (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Within the cortex, the somatosensory, motor, and visual cortices had the highest enrichment score for both groups of infected mice.
source: For both groups of infected mice, within the cortex, the somatosensory, motor, and visual cortices had the highest enrichment score (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cerebellum and the white matter tracts showed a significant lack of enrichment in both II-Cre and III-Cre infected mice.
source: Finally, two regions—the cerebellum and the white matter tracts—showed a significant lack of enrichment in both II-Cre and III-Cre infected mice (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The lack of TINs in white matter tracts is expected given that these tracts are primarily made up of neuron axons and thus have a paucity of neuron nuclei.
source: The lack of TINs in white matter tracts is expected given that these tracts are primarily made up of neuron axons and thus have a paucity of neuron nuclei, the cellular component by which neurons are anatomically mapped.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the composition of white matter tracts.

claim: TINs localization in the striatum is consistent with its size.
source: While TINs localization in the striatum is consistent with its size, the enrichment of TINs in the cortex and lack of TINs in the cerebellum are not accounted for by the relative size of these regions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the enrichment index analysis shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The enrichment of TINs in the cortex is not accounted for by the relative size of the cortex.
source: While TINs localization in the striatum is consistent with its size, the enrichment of TINs in the cortex and lack of TINs in the cerebellum are not accounted for by the relative size of these regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the enrichment index analysis shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The lack of TINs in the cerebellum is not accounted for by the relative size of the cerebellum.
source: While TINs localization in the striatum is consistent with its size, the enrichment of TINs in the cortex and lack of TINs in the cerebellum are not accounted for by the relative size of these regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the enrichment index analysis shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Prior work suggested that Toxoplasma infection might specifically affect inhibitory neurons.
source: Given that prior work suggested that Toxoplasma infection might specifically affect inhibitory neurons (Brooks et al., 2015), we first examined how often TINs co-localized with two common markers for inhibitory interneurons, calbindin and parvalbumin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: GAD+ interneurons make up approximately 15–20% of all cortical neurons.
source: We chose these makers rather than the pan-inhibitory marker glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) [GAD+ interneurons make up approximately 15–20% of all cortical neurons (Gentet et al., 2000; Lodato and Arlotta, 2015)] as GAD staining is altered in Toxoplasma-infected brain (Brooks et al., 2015; Carrillo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: GAD staining is altered in Toxoplasma-infected brain.
source: We chose these makers rather than the pan-inhibitory marker glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) [GAD+ interneurons make up approximately 15–20% of all cortical neurons (Gentet et al., 2000; Lodato and Arlotta, 2015)] as GAD staining is altered in Toxoplasma-infected brain (Brooks et al., 2015; Carrillo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Parvalbumin labels 40–50% of GAD+ interneurons.
source: Fortunately, parvalbumin labels 40–50% of GAD+ interneurons and calbindin labels approximately 30% of GAD+ interneurons (Hof et al., 1999; Keller et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Calbindin labels approximately 30% of GAD+ interneurons.
source: Fortunately, parvalbumin labels 40–50% of GAD+ interneurons and calbindin labels approximately 30% of GAD+ interneurons (Hof et al., 1999; Keller et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Within the cortex, approximately 5% (4.8 ± 2.0% II-Cre, 3.9 ± 0.6% III-Cre) of TINs were calbindin+.
source: Within the cortex, irrespective of infecting strain, approximately 5% (4.8 ± 2.0% II-Cre, 3.9 ± 0.6% III-Cre) of TINs were calbindin+ (Figure 2A,B), while none were parvalbumin+ (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Within the cortex, no TINs were parvalbumin+.
source: Within the cortex, irrespective of infecting strain, approximately 5% (4.8 ± 2.0% II-Cre, 3.9 ± 0.6% III-Cre) of TINs were calbindin+ (Figure 2A,B), while none were parvalbumin+ (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: In the striatum, approximately 4% of II-Cre TINs were calbindin+ (4.4 ± 2.0%).
source: In the striatum, we observed that approximately 4% of II-Cre TINs were calbindin+ (4.4 ± 2.0%) and approximately 9% of III-Cre TINs were calbindin+ (9.4 ± 3.4%) (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: In the striatum, approximately 9% of III-Cre TINs were calbindin+ (9.4 ± 3.4%).
source: In the striatum, we observed that approximately 4% of II-Cre TINs were calbindin+ (4.4 ± 2.0%) and approximately 9% of III-Cre TINs were calbindin+ (9.4 ± 3.4%) (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: No TINs co-localized with parvalbumin+ neurons in the striatum.
source: As in the cortex, no TINs co-localized with parvalbumin+ neurons in the striatum (N = 6–65 TINs/mouse, four mice for II-Cre; N = 30 and 84 TINs/mouse, two mice for III-Cre).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescent assays.

claim: Toxoplasma rarely interacts with or injects cortical or striatal interneurons.
source: These data suggest that Toxoplasma rarely interacts with or injects cortical or striatal interneurons, though we cannot exclude the possibility that Toxoplasma-injected interneurons die prior to the expression of GFP or that parasites primarily interact with interneurons that do not express parvalbumin or calbindin.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the low co-localization rates between TINs and interneuron markers shown in Figure 2.

claim: Within interneurons, Toxoplasma more commonly injects calbindin+ interneurons, not parvalbumin+ interneurons.
source: Within interneurons, Toxoplasma more commonly injects calbindin+ interneurons, not parvalbumin+ interneurons, an unexpected finding given the higher prevalence of parvalbumin+ interneurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2, where some TINs co-localize with calbindin but none with parvalbumin.

claim: FoxP2 is primarily expressed by glutamatergic/excitatory neurons within layer 6 of the mouse cortex.
source: FoxP2 is primarily expressed by glutamatergic/excitatory neurons within layer 6 of the mouse cortex, though some FoxP2+ excitatory neurons are also found in cortical layers IV and V (Arlotta et al., 2005; Lodato and Arlotta, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some FoxP2+ excitatory neurons are also found in cortical layers IV and V.
source: FoxP2 is primarily expressed by glutamatergic/excitatory neurons within layer 6 of the mouse cortex, though some FoxP2+ excitatory neurons are also found in cortical layers IV and V (Arlotta et al., 2005; Lodato and Arlotta, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: FoxP2 expression occurs in medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the striatum.
source: FoxP2 expression also occurs in medium spiny neurons (MSNs) in the striatum, allowing us to use a single marker for both cortical and striatal studies (Ferland et al., 2003; Lai et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Within the cortex, approximately 58% (58.0 ± 3.8% II-Cre, 58.3 ± 2.3% III-Cre) of the analyzed TINs showed FoxP2 co-localization.
source: Within the cortex, irrespective of infecting Toxoplasma strain, approximately 58% (58.0 ± 3.8% II-Cre, 58.3 ± 2.3% III-Cre) of the analyzed TINs showed FoxP2 co-localization (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In the striatum, approximately 68% (68.1 ± 7.2%) of analyzed II-Cre TINs showed FoxP2 co-localization.
source: In the striatum, we found that approximately 68% (68.1 ± 7.2%) of analyzed II-Cre TINs and approximately 83% (83 ± 4.1%) of analyzed III-Cre TINs showed FoxP2 co-localization (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: In the striatum, approximately 83% (83 ± 4.1%) of analyzed III-Cre TINs showed FoxP2 co-localization.
source: In the striatum, we found that approximately 68% (68.1 ± 7.2%) of analyzed II-Cre TINs and approximately 83% (83 ± 4.1%) of analyzed III-Cre TINs showed FoxP2 co-localization (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: 90–95% of neurons in the striatum are MSNs.
source: This high rate of co-localization between striatal TINs and FoxP2 suggested that striatal TINs were MSNs, which would be expected given that 90–95% of neurons in the striatum are MSNs (Ouimet et al., 1984; Ouimet and Greengard, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Approximately 20% (19.9 ± 5.7%) of II-Cre striatal TINs co-localized with DARPP32+ staining.
source: We found that approximately 20% (19.9 ± 5.7%) of II-Cre striatal TINs and approximately 25% (23.6 ± 4.8%) of III-Cre striatal TINs co-localized with DARPP32+ staining (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Approximately 25% (23.6 ± 4.8%) of III-Cre striatal TINs co-localized with DARPP32+ staining.
source: We found that approximately 20% (19.9 ± 5.7%) of II-Cre striatal TINs and approximately 25% (23.6 ± 4.8%) of III-Cre striatal TINs co-localized with DARPP32+ staining (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Toxoplasma infection alters protein localization and expression.
source: Given the relatively low percentage of TINs co-localizing with DARPP32 and prior work suggesting Toxoplasma infection alters protein localization and expression (Cekanaviciute et al., 2014; Brooks et al., 2015; David et al., 2016), we sought to determine how striatal FoxP2 and DARPP32 staining differed between uninfected and infected mice, and if this staining differed by proximity to TINs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The average number of FoxP2+ neurons in each image did not differ between images from either uninfected or infected mice, regardless of infecting Toxoplasma strain.
source: We found that the average number of FoxP2+ neurons in each image did not differ between images from either uninfected or infected mice, regardless of infecting Toxoplasma strain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A); nor did the abundance vary in proximity to TINs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The abundance of FoxP2+ neurons did not vary in proximity to TINs.
source: We found that the average number of FoxP2+ neurons in each image did not differ between images from either uninfected or infected mice, regardless of infecting Toxoplasma strain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A); nor did the abundance vary in proximity to TINs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The average number of DARPP32+ neurons in each image did not differ between random images from uninfected or infected mice.
source: The average number of DARPP32+ neurons in each image also did not differ between random images from uninfected or infected mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In images taken in proximity to TINs, the number of DARPP32+ neurons showed a statistically significant decrease.
source: Conversely, in images taken in proximity to TINs, the number of DARPP32+ neurons showed a statistically significant decrease (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: On average, more striatal neurons were FoxP2+ than DARPP32+, even in uninfected mice.
source: In addition, we noted that, on average, more striatal neurons were FoxP2+ than DARPP32+, even in uninfected mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: Only approximately 70% of FoxP2+ neurons stained for DARPP32 (69.6 ± 0.3% saline, 68.6 ± 0.6% II-Cre, 73.0 ± 4.0% III-Cre).
source: Consistent with the findings in the single stains, only approximately 70% of FoxP2+ neurons stained for DARPP32 (69.6 ± 0.3% saline, 68.6 ± 0.6% II-Cre, 73.0 ± 4.0% III-Cre) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), while 99% (99.7 ± 0.0% saline, 99.8 ± 0.0% II-Cre, 99.8 ± 0.1% III-Cre) of DARPP32+ neurons stained for FoxP2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 99% (99.7 ± 0.0% saline, 99.8 ± 0.0% II-Cre, 99.8 ± 0.1% III-Cre) of DARPP32+ neurons stained for FoxP2.
source: Consistent with the findings in the single stains, only approximately 70% of FoxP2+ neurons stained for DARPP32 (69.6 ± 0.3% saline, 68.6 ± 0.6% II-Cre, 73.0 ± 4.0% III-Cre) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), while 99% (99.7 ± 0.0% saline, 99.8 ± 0.0% II-Cre, 99.8 ± 0.1% III-Cre) of DARPP32+ neurons stained for FoxP2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Striatal TINs are likely MSNs as they co-localize with markers of MSNs, especially FoxP2.
source: These data suggest that striatal TINs are likely MSNs as they co-localize with markers of MSNs, especially FoxP2.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-localization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The higher co-localization of TINs with FoxP2 versus DARPP32 is likely driven by the higher number of FoxP2+ neurons within the striatum as well as the sensitivity of DARPP32 expression/staining to disruption by infection or inflammation.
source: The higher co-localization of TINs with FoxP2 versus DARPP32 is likely driven by the higher number of FoxP2+ neurons within the striatum as well as the sensitivity of DARPP32 expression/staining to disruption by infection or inflammation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: FoxP2 may be a more sensitive marker for striatal MSNs than DARPP32.
source: Given that FoxP2 stains more striatal neurons than DARPP32, even in uninfected mice, FoxP2 may be a more sensitive marker for striatal MSNs than DARPP32.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing that FoxP2 labels more striatal neurons than DARPP32.

claim: MSNs make up 90–95% of dorsal striatal neurons.
source: MSNs make up 90–95% of dorsal striatal neurons (Mensah and Deadwyler, 1974; Graveland and DiFiglia, 1985; Gerfen, 1992) and are highly characterized, including at the level of single cell electrophysiology in situ (i.e., patch clamping in ex vivo slices).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bystander MSNs had a resting membrane potential of −69.0 ± 1.2 mV, which is mildly depolarized compared to MSNs in uninfected mice.
source: Bystander MSNs had a resting membrane potential of −69.0 ± 1.2 mV, which is mildly depolarized compared to MSNs in uninfected mice (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Bystander MSNs required fewer steps of injected current to reach the threshold to fire the first AP compared to MSNs in uninfected mice (12 ± 0.3 steps for bystanders and 13 ± 0.4 for MSNs in uninfected mice).
source: Consistent with a depolarized resting membrane potential, bystander MSNs required fewer steps of injected current to reach the threshold to fire the first AP compared to MSNs in uninfected mice (12 ± 0.3 steps for bystanders and 13 ± 0.4 for MSNs in uninfected mice) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: AP threshold, after hyperpolarization peak, AP amplitude, delay to first AP, and input resistance were equivalent when comparing bystander MSNs to MSNs from uninfected mice.
source: Besides these two properties, the following electrophysiologic properties were equivalent when comparing bystander MSNs to MSNs from uninfected mice: AP threshold, after hyperpolarization peak, AP amplitude, delay to first AP, and input resistance (Figure 5B–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B–G.

claim: The infected/inflammatory microenvironment at this time point causes relatively little change to neurons that have not directly interacted with Toxoplasma.
source: These results indicate that though there is a mild change in the resting membrane potential of bystander MSNs during infection, the infected/inflammatory microenvironment at this time point causes relatively little change to neurons that have not directly interacted with Toxoplasma.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the electrophysiology data comparing bystander MSNs to uninfected MSNs shown in Figure 5.

claim: Most striatal TINs had highly depolarized resting membrane potentials (−49.1 ± 4.5 mV) compared to either bystander or uninfected MSNs.
source: Unexpectedly, we were unable to properly patch onto most striatal TINs (i.e., we were unable to form a gigaseal). We were able to record from a total of 10 TINs, most of which had highly depolarized resting membrane potentials (−49.1 ± 4.5 mV) compared to either bystander or uninfected MSNs (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: None of the recorded TINs generated APs in response to the standard protocol.
source: None of these TINs generated APs in response to the standard protocol, possibly because this highly depolarized membrane potential is too close to the threshold for firing an AP (~45 mV) in MSNs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: After hyperpolarization, TINs could generate APs.
source: For five TINs, after we applied between −20 and −180 pA of negative current, membrane potentials of −55 to −66 mV were observed. With this 'normalization' of the resting membrane potential, we found that TINs could generate APs (Figure 6B), definitively showing that they were neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The depolarized resting membrane potential of TINs was not due to fluorescent protein expression in the setting of inflammation.
source: Finally, to ensure the depolarized resting membrane potential of TINs was not due to fluorescent protein expression in the setting of inflammation, we recorded from YFP+ neurons in infected mice that constitutively express YFP in a subset of cortical neurons (Feng et al., 2000). In these mice, we found a range of resting membrane potentials that is typical of cortical neurons (Pangratz-Fuehrer and Hestrin, 2011; Oswald et al., 2013) and distinct from the physiologic abnormalities observed in TINs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Brain sections from 8 wpi mice showed an approximately 90% reduction in the number of TINs compared to brain sections from three wpi mice.
source: Given that such findings are consistent with the electrophysiology of sick or dying neurons (Lipton, 1999), we compared the total number of TINs in brain sections from mice infected with III-Cre parasites for 3 or 8 weeks. Consistent with the possibility that the electrophysiology reflects that TINs are sick/dying, brain sections from 8 wpi mice showed an approximately 90% reduction in the number of TINs compared to brain sections from three wpi mice (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Neurons that directly interact with Toxoplasma have highly aberrant electrophysiology and most will die over a relatively short period.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that neurons that directly interact with Toxoplasma have highly aberrant electrophysiology and most will die over a relatively short period.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of electrophysiology data (Figure 6) and TIN survival data (Figure 7).

claim: Bystander neurons show relatively minor changes in terms of electrophysiology.
source: On the other hand, bystander neurons, which are in a similar inflammatory environment, show relatively minor changes in terms of electrophysiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Neuron pathology is extremely targeted, even in a highly inflammatory setting.
source: Together, these data suggest that neuron pathology is extremely targeted, even in a highly inflammatory setting.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of TIN and bystander electrophysiology.

claim: TINs consistently localize to the cortex and striatum across multiple cohorts of mice and using two genetically distinct Toxoplasma strains.
source: Across multiple cohorts of mice and using two genetically distinct Toxoplasma strains, our data show that TINs consistently localize to the cortex and striatum.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: For the cortex, the number of TINs is higher than would be expected even after accounting for the size of the cortex.
source: For the cortex, the number of TINs is higher than would be expected even after accounting for the size of the cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the enrichment index data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: There is little evidence of Toxoplasma targeting a specific neuron subtype within the cortex and striatum.
source: Within the cortex and striatum, we found little evidence of Toxoplasma targeting a specific neuron subtype, as TINs co-localize with markers for highly abundant neurons in a region (e.g., MSNs in the striatum).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-localization data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Bystander MSNs showed mild changes in resting membrane potential and no changes in other passive firing properties.
source: Bystander MSNs showed mild changes in resting membrane potential and no changes in other passive firing properties, while TINs had highly depolarized resting membrane potentials and did not fire APs unless artificially hyperpolarized.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5.

claim: TINs had highly depolarized resting membrane potentials and did not fire APs unless artificially hyperpolarized.
source: Bystander MSNs showed mild changes in resting membrane potential and no changes in other passive firing properties, while TINs had highly depolarized resting membrane potentials and did not fire APs unless artificially hyperpolarized.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6.

claim: TINs are unhealthy and potentially dying.
source: These data suggest that TINs, but not bystanders, are unhealthy and potentially dying, a possibility confirmed by a drastic decrease in the number of TINs by 8 wpi.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of aberrant electrophysiology (Figure 6) and decreased TIN numbers over time (Figure 7).

claim: The drastic decrease in the number of TINs by 8 wpi confirms that TINs are unhealthy and potentially dying.
source: These data suggest that TINs, but not bystanders, are unhealthy and potentially dying, a possibility confirmed by a drastic decrease in the number of TINs by 8 wpi.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The cortex and especially the motor, somatosensory, visual cortical regions show enrichment for Toxoplasma presence (TINs or cysts) even when accounting for region size.
source: All three studies found: (i) high levels of inter-mouse variability; (ii) identified the cortex—and especially the motor, somatosensory, visual cortical regions—as showing enrichment for Toxoplasma presence (TINs or cysts) even when accounting for region size; and (iii) determined that the cerebellum shows relatively little Toxoplasma presence, especially when accounting for size.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior studies and the current study's data.

claim: The cerebellum shows relatively little Toxoplasma presence, especially when accounting for size.
source: All three studies found: (i) high levels of inter-mouse variability; (ii) identified the cortex—and especially the motor, somatosensory, visual cortical regions—as showing enrichment for Toxoplasma presence (TINs or cysts) even when accounting for region size; and (iii) determined that the cerebellum shows relatively little Toxoplasma presence, especially when accounting for size.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with prior studies and the current study's data.

claim: Regional cyst burden is driven by differences in the number of neuron-parasite interactions, not by differences in regional innate immune responses.
source: These consistencies suggest that regional cyst burden is driven by differences in the number of neuron-parasite interactions, not by differences in regional innate immune responses as has been suggested for West Nile virus (WNV) infection (Cho et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the consistency between TIN distribution and cyst distribution across studies.

claim: These regional differences are consistent with the largest studies in AIDS patients with toxoplasmic encephalitis, in which more lesions are identified in the cortex and the basal ganglia compared to the cerebellum.
source: In addition, these regional differences are consistent with the largest studies in AIDS patients with toxoplasmic encephalitis, in which more lesions are identified in the cortex and the basal ganglia compared to the cerebellum (Porter and Sande, 1992; Arendt et al., 1999), highlighting the relevance of the mouse model to human disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: One possibility for regional differences in tropism is differences in the transmissibility of Toxoplasma across the vasculature that supplies the cortex and striatum/basal ganglia versus the cerebellum.
source: Currently, we do not know what drives these regional differences in tropism, though one possibility is differences in the transmissibility of Toxoplasma across the vasculature that supplies the cortex and striatum/basal ganglia versus the cerebellum (anterior versus posterior circulation, respectively), a possibility also suggested for WNV (Daniels et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: TINs are comprised of common neuron subtypes in the deep cortex and striatum.
source: The finding that TINs are comprised of common neuron subtypes in the deep cortex and striatum (e.g., FoxP2+ neurons) suggests that Toxoplasma injects (and presumptively infects) in proportion to the neuron subtypes in a given region.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the co-localization data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Toxoplasma injects (and presumptively infects) in proportion to the neuron subtypes in a given region.
source: The finding that TINs are comprised of common neuron subtypes in the deep cortex and striatum (e.g., FoxP2+ neurons) suggests that Toxoplasma injects (and presumptively infects) in proportion to the neuron subtypes in a given region.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TINs co-localize with abundant neuron markers.

claim: One exception to the rule that Toxoplasma injects in proportion to neuron subtypes is the lack of TINs that also express parvalbumin.
source: One exception to this rule is the lack of TINs that also express parvalbumin.
evidence: This claim is supported by the co-localization data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Parvalbumin-expressing neurons make up approximately 40–50% of the cortical GABAergic (inhibitory) neurons and are found in all deeper layers of the cortex.
source: Parvalbumin-expressing neurons make up approximately 40–50% of the cortical GABAergic (inhibitory) neurons and are found in all deeper layers of the cortex, while calbindin-expressing neurons are less frequent, especially in layers IV-VI of the cortex (Hof et al., 1999; Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Calbindin-expressing neurons are less frequent than parvalbumin-expressing neurons, especially in layers IV-VI of the cortex.
source: Parvalbumin-expressing neurons make up approximately 40–50% of the cortical GABAergic (inhibitory) neurons and are found in all deeper layers of the cortex, while calbindin-expressing neurons are less frequent, especially in layers IV-VI of the cortex (Hof et al., 1999; Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: One possibility for the lack of parvalbumin+ TINs is a decrease or change in parvalbumin expression/location.
source: One possibility for the lack of parvalbumin+ TINs is a decrease or change in parvalbumin expression/location as seen for DARPP-32 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or GAD-67 (Brooks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: Another possibility is that parvalbumin+ neurons have fewer interactions with Toxoplasma because they have a high concentration of perineural nets blocking Toxoplasma's ability to contact parvalbumin+ neurons.
source: Another more exciting possibility is that parvalbumin+ neurons have fewer interactions with Toxoplasma because they have a high concentration of perineural nets—extracellular matrix that surrounds different parts of the neuron (Baker et al., 2017)—blocking Toxoplasma's ability to contact parvalbumin+ neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: Another possibility is that parvalbumin+ neurons are highly sensitive to injection with Toxoplasma protein and rapidly die before expressing GFP and/or die prior to the time point at which studies were performed.
source: Another possibility is that parvalbumin+ neurons are highly sensitive to injection with Toxoplasma protein and rapidly die before expressing GFP and/or die prior to the time point at which we performed our studies.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: These studies are the first in any neurotropic infection to compare the in situ electrophysiology between microbe-interacted (or infected) neurons versus those neurons in close proximity but without direct microbial interactions.
source: To the best of our knowledge, these studies are the first in any neurotropic infection to compare the in situ electrophysiology between microbe-interacted (or infected) neurons versus those neurons in close proximity but without direct microbial interactions.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Microglia will strip synapses off infected and uninfected neurons in the inflamed brain.
source: Given the relatively common understanding that microglia will strip synapses off infected and uninfected neurons in the inflamed brain (Vasek et al., 2016; Di Liberto et al., 2018), we found it remarkable that bystander MSNs physiology showed only minor changes compared to MSNs from uninfected mice while TINs showed highly abnormal electrophysiology (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: One possible explanation for the minimal changes seen in bystanders is that these neurons undergo compensatory mechanisms that allow them to avoid drastically changing.
source: One possible explanation for the minimal changes seen in bystanders is that these neurons undergo compensatory mechanisms that allow them to avoid drastically changing, as a dramatic response would be detrimental to the local circuitry.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: Another possibility is that the effect of the neuroinflammatory response is confined to a small area near TINs, leaving more distant bystanders relatively spared.
source: Another possibility is that the effect of the neuroinflammatory response is confined to a small area near TINs, leaving these more distant bystanders relatively spared.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: The depolarized resting membrane potential of bystanders is abnormal and the decrease in required input current suggests these neurons are mildly hyperexcitable.
source: Of note, while the physiology of the bystanders is relatively normal compared to TINs, this depolarized resting membrane potential is still abnormal and the decrease in required input current (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) suggests these neurons are mildly hyperexcitable.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: If similar changes occur in other bystander neurons and in other CNS infections, they might explain why patients with active brain infections have an increased likelihood of seizing.
source: If similar changes also occur in other bystander neurons (e.g., cortical neurons) and in other CNS infections, they might explain why patients with active brain infections have an increased likelihood of seizing (Luft and Remington, 1992; Neu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential clinical implications.

claim: Mild abnormalities in bystander neurons might summate across many bystander neurons to cause circuit level changes.
source: These mild abnormalities might also summate across many bystander neurons to cause circuit level changes.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: Changes in the far more numerous bystanders could explain both the heterogeneity of behavioral changes seen in infected animals and the relative lack of behavioral abnormalities observed in Toxoplasma-infected mice that have cleared both the infection and the immune response.
source: While we did not test this possibility, such changes in the far more numerous bystanders—especially if the changes are reversible—could explain both the heterogeneity of behavioral changes seen in infected animals (Worth et al., 2014) and the relative lack of behavioral abnormalities observed in Toxoplasma-infected mice that have cleared both the infection and the immune response (McGovern et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential behavioral implications.

claim: TINs include actively infected neurons and uninfected, injected neurons.
source: TINs—which include actively infected neurons and uninfected, injected neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)—show highly abnormal electrophysiology, only firing APs after artificial hyperpolarization.
evidence: This claim is based on prior work by the authors' group.

claim: The root cause of abnormal physiology in TINs is specific to neurons injected with Toxoplasma protein.
source: While we cannot distinguish between whether this abnormal physiology leads to neuron death or the sick state of these neurons drives the abnormal physiology (we favor the latter possibility), the discrepancy between the physiology of TINs and bystanders suggests that the root cause is specific to neurons injected with Toxoplasma protein.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of TIN and bystander electrophysiology.

claim: Restricted changes in TINs could arise from direct manipulation of TINs by the injected parasite proteins.
source: Such restricted changes could arise from direct manipulation of TINs by the injected parasite proteins or selective microglial/macrophage recognition and phagocytosis of TINs, consistent with what was observed in lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus infection (Di Liberto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: Restricted changes in TINs could arise from selective microglial/macrophage recognition and phagocytosis of TINs.
source: Such restricted changes could arise from direct manipulation of TINs by the injected parasite proteins or selective microglial/macrophage recognition and phagocytosis of TINs, consistent with what was observed in lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus infection (Di Liberto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: Another possibility is that the immune response is tightly regulated and confined, such that the destruction leveled by this response is limited to a very small area around TINs.
source: Another possibility, as noted above, is that the immune response is tightly regulated and confined, such that the destruction leveled by this response is limited to a very small area around TINs.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: Partial abrogation of astrocytic TGF-β signaling led to de-regulation of the CNS immune response to Toxoplasma and higher levels of neuronal loss without changing the CNS parasite burden.
source: Such a possibility is consistent with prior work showing that partial abrogation of astrocytic TGF-β signaling led to de-regulation of the CNS immune response to Toxoplasma and higher levels of neuronal loss without changing the CNS parasite burden (Cekanaviciute et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The finding of an approximately 90% decrease in TINs by 8 wpi suggests that we need to re-evaluate our understanding of how and why microbes persist in or even infect neurons.
source: Finally, our finding of an approximately 90% decrease in TINs by 8 wpi suggests that we need to re-evaluate our understanding of how and why microbes persist in or even infect neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TIN survival data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Microbes with the capability to infect multiple cell types are commonly found in neurons, not astrocytes.
source: Microbes with the capability to infect multiple cell types are commonly found in neurons, not astrocytes (e.g., Toxoplasma, WNV, measles virus).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about neurotropic microbes.

claim: This neuronal preference has been explained by the idea that neurons survive infection through non-cytolytic clearance of microbes and/or pushing the infecting microbes to enter a latent state.
source: This neuronal preference has been explained by the idea that—given the long-lived, relatively non-regenerative nature of neurons—neuron survival must be ensured at almost any cost. Thus, rather than initiating an immune response that might result in neuron death, neurons survive infection through non-cytolytic clearance of microbes (Binder and Griffin, 2001; Patterson et al., 2002; Samuel and Diamond, 2005; Miller et al., 2016) and/or pushing the infecting microbes to enter a latent state (Speck and Simmons, 1991; Ferguson and Hutchison, 1987; Tanaka et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The death of TINs directly challenges the model that neuron survival must be ensured at almost any cost.
source: The death of TINs directly challenges this model, suggesting that the battle to persist in neurons is far more nuanced than previously recognized.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TINs die over time.

claim: Given that >90% of TINs are expected to be uninfected, many uninfected neurons are dying.
source: For example, given that >90% of TINs are expected to be uninfected (Koshy et al., 2012), we would predict that many uninfected neurons are dying.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of prior data on TIN composition and current data on TIN death.

claim: One possibility is that uninfected, parasite-manipulated neurons are so abnormal that global brain function is better preserved with the removal of these neurons.
source: One possibility is that these TINs are so abnormal (from either direct manipulation by parasites or because of neuron-immune cell interactions) that global brain function is better preserved with the removal of these neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: Such a possibility is consistent with the altered gene expression identified in neurons that cleared an attenuated rabies virus infection.
source: Such a possibility is consistent with the altered gene expression identified in neurons that cleared an attenuated rabies virus infection (Gomme et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Another possibility is that the death of TINs is essential for parasite control and perhaps the death of uninfected TINs is simply collateral damage.
source: Another possibility is that the death of TINs—both infected and uninfected—is essential for parasite control and perhaps the death of uninfected TINs is simply collateral damage.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: The death of uninfected TINs might divert immune attention from the rare, persistently infected neuron.
source: Or the death of uninfected TINs might divert immune attention from the rare, persistently infected neuron.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: An alternative model for neuron-tropic microbes is that neurons mount appropriate immune responses to both cytokines and infections such that persistent infection is a rare outcome, rather than a universal one.
source: Regardless of whether this death benefits the host or microbe (or both), based upon the data presented here and previously, we offer an alternative model for neuron-tropic microbes: neurons mount appropriate immune responses to both cytokines and infections such that persistent infection is a rare outcome, rather than a universal one.
evidence: This is a speculative claim proposing an alternative model based on the study's findings.

claim: Limited data in a murine model of measles virus infection is consistent with the alternative model that persistent infection is a rare outcome.
source: Limited data in a murine model of measles virus infection is consistent with this possibility (Miller et al., 2019), though future studies using other neurotropic pathogens will be required to definitively determine how universal this model is.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Over 90% of TINs do not harbor parasites.
source: TINs (GFP+) include both infected and uninfected neurons, with over 90% of TINs not harboring parasites (Koshy et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors' group.

claim: During recordings, no TINs with a cyst were observed.
source: During recordings, no TINs with a cyst were observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the electrophysiology experiments.
